prompt: In a pile of 200 coins, 2% are gold coins and the rest are silver. Simple Simon removes one silver coin every day until the pile contains 20% gold coins. How many silver coins does Simon remove?

solutions.title: Gold coins stay fixed
solutions.body:
There are $0.02\times200=4$ gold coins, and this number never changes. In the final pile they are $20\%$, so the final pile has $4\times5=20$ coins. Simon removes $200-20=180$ silver coins.

**Answer: 180**

solutions.title: Solve an equation
solutions.body:
After $s$ days the pile has $200-s$ coins and $4$ of them are gold: $4=0.2(200-s)$, so $200-s=20$ and $s=180$.

**Answer: 180**

prompt: The value of the expression $1+\dfrac{1}{1+\dfrac{1}{1+\frac15}}$ is $\dfrac ab$, where $a$ and $b$ are integers whose only common factor is 1. What is the value of $a+b$?

solutions.title: Simplify from the inside
solutions.body:
$1+\frac15=\frac65$, so $\frac{1}{1+1/5}=\frac56$. Then $1+\frac56=\frac{11}6$, so the next fraction is $\frac6{11}$, and $1+\frac6{11}=\frac{17}{11}$. Since $\gcd(17,11)=1$, $a+b=17+11=28$.

**Answer: 28**

prompt: The diagram shows a solid with six triangular faces and five vertices. Andrew wants to write an integer at each of the vertices so that the sum of the numbers at the three vertices of each face is the same. He has already written the numbers 1 and 5 as shown. What is the sum of the other three numbers he will write?

solutions.title: Compare faces
solutions.body:
Call the three unknown vertices $x,y,z$ (with $z$ the lowest vertex). Three faces meet at the vertex $1$ and contain the vertices $\{1,5,x\}$, $\{1,x,y\}$, $\{1,5,y\}$. Equal sums give $x=y=5$, so every face sum is $1+5+5=11$. The bottom face contains $x,y,z$, so $x+y+z=11$.

**Answer: 11**

prompt: A box contains two white socks, three blue socks and four grey socks. Rachel knows that three of the socks have holes in, but does not know what colour these socks are. She takes one sock at a time from the box without looking. How many socks must she take for her to be certain she has a pair of socks of the same colour without holes?

solutions.title: Pigeonhole
solutions.body:
Six socks are not enough: they could be the three socks with holes plus one hole-free sock of each colour, giving no hole-free pair.

Seven socks are enough: at most $3$ of them have holes, so at least $4$ are hole-free, and with only $3$ colours two of those four have the same colour.

**Answer: 7**

prompt: The diagram shows two circles and a square with sides of length 10 cm. One vertex of the square is at the centre of the large circle and two sides of the square are tangents to both circles. The small circle touches the large circle. The radius of the small circle is $(a-b\sqrt2)$ cm. What is the value of $a+b$?

solutions.title: Use the diagonal
solutions.body:
Let $O$ be the centre of the large circle (radius $10$, the side of the square) and $Q$ the opposite corner of the square, so $OQ=10\sqrt2$. Let the small circle have radius $r$ and centre $P$. It is tangent to the two sides through $Q$, so $P$ lies on diagonal $OQ$ with $PQ=r\sqrt2$. The circles touch externally, so $OP=10+r$. Hence
$$10+r+r\sqrt2=10\sqrt2\ \Rightarrow\ r=\frac{10(\sqrt2-1)}{\sqrt2+1}=10(\sqrt2-1)^2=30-20\sqrt2.$$
So $a=30$, $b=20$ and $a+b=50$.

**Answer: 50**

prompt: The median of a set of five positive integers is one more than the mode and one less than the mean. What is the largest possible value of the range of the five integers?

solutions.title: Set up the ordered list
solutions.body:
Let the integers be $p\le q\le r\le s\le t$. The median is $r$ and the mode is $r-1$, so the value $r-1$ appears at least twice: $p=q=r-1$ (and no other value repeats, so $r<s<t$). The mean is $r+1$, so the total is $5r+5$:
$$(r-1)+(r-1)+r+s+t=5r+5\ \Rightarrow\ s+t=2r+7.$$
Since $s\ge r+1$, the largest $t$ is $2r+7-(r+1)=r+6$. The range is at most $t-p=(r+6)-(r-1)=7$, and e.g. $r=3$: $2,2,3,4,9$ gives median 3, mode 2, mean 4 and range 7.

**Answer: 7**

prompt: The diagram shows a triangle $ABC$ with area $12\text{ cm}^2$. The sides of the triangle are extended to points $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$, $T$ and $U$ as shown so that $PA=AB=BS$, $QA=AC=CT$ and $RB=BC=CU$. What is the area (in $\text{cm}^2$) of hexagon $PQRSTU$?

solutions.title: Add up the pieces
solutions.body:
Triangle $AST$ is similar to $ABC$ with ratio $2:1$ (since $SA=2BA$, $TA=2CA$), so its area is $4\times12=48$; removing $ABC$ leaves $36$ for the quadrilateral $BSTC$. In the same way the quadrilaterals $CUPA$ and $AQRB$ each have area $36$.

Triangles $APQ$ and $ABC$ are congruent (SAS: $AP=AB$, $AQ=AC$, vertically opposite angles at $A$), so $APQ$ has area $12$; likewise $BRS$ and $CTU$ have area $12$.

The hexagon consists of $ABC$ ($12$), the three quadrilaterals ($3\times36=108$) and the three outer triangles ($3\times12=36$): $12+108+36=156$.

**Answer: 156**

prompt: A mob of 2015 kangaroos contains only red and grey kangaroos. One grey kangaroo is taller than exactly one red kangaroo, one grey kangaroo is taller than exactly three red kangaroos, one grey kangaroo is taller than exactly five red kangaroos and so on with each successive grey kangaroo being taller than exactly two more red kangaroos than the previous grey kangaroo. The final grey kangaroo is taller than all the red kangaroos. How many grey kangaroos are in the mob?

solutions.title: Let the number of greys be $g$
solutions.body:
The $k$-th grey kangaroo is taller than exactly $2k-1$ red kangaroos. The last one ($k=g$) is taller than all the reds, so there are $2g-1$ red kangaroos. Then $g+(2g-1)=2015$, so $3g=2016$ and $g=672$.

**Answer: 672**

prompt: A large rectangle is divided into four identical smaller rectangles by slicing parallel to one of its sides. The perimeter of the large rectangle is 18 metres more than the perimeter of each of the smaller rectangles. The area of the large rectangle is $18\text{ m}^2$ more than the area of each of the smaller rectangles. What is the perimeter in metres of the large rectangle?

solutions.title: Two equations
solutions.body:
Let the large rectangle be $x$ by $y$, cut into four pieces of size $\frac x4$ by $y$. Perimeters: $2x+2y=2\cdot\frac x4+2y+18$, so $\frac{3x}2=18$ and $x=12$. Areas: $xy=\frac x4y+18$, so $12y=3y+18$ and $y=2$. The perimeter is $2(12+2)=28$ m.

**Answer: 28**

prompt: Katherine and James are jogging in the same direction around a pond. They start at the same time and from the same place and each jogs at a constant speed. Katherine, the faster jogger, takes 3 minutes to complete one lap and first overtakes James 8 minutes after starting. How many seconds does it take James to complete one lap?

A ball is propelled from corner $A$ of a square snooker table of side 2 metres. After bouncing off three cushions as shown, the ball goes into a pocket at $B$. The total distance travelled by the ball is $\sqrt k$ metres. What is the value of $k$? (When the ball bounces off a cushion, the angle its path makes with the cushion as it approaches the point of impact is equal to the angle its path makes with the cushion as it moves away from the point of impact.)

solutions.title: Reflect the table
solutions.body:
Instead of bouncing, unfold the path by reflecting the table in each cushion the ball hits. The path becomes a straight segment from $A$ to a reflected copy $B'$ of $B$. Along the path the ball travels $2+1+1+2=6$ m horizontally in total and $2+2=4$ m vertically in total (it goes up the full height of the table once and down once), so the straight unfolded segment has length $\sqrt{6^2+4^2}=\sqrt{52}$ metres.

**Answer: 52**

prompt: Chris planned a 210 km bike ride. However, he rode 5 km/h faster than he planned and finished his ride 1 hour earlier than he planned. His average speed for the ride was $x$ km/h. What is the value of $x$?

solutions.title: Time equation
solutions.body:
Planned speed $x-5$, actual speed $x$:
$$\frac{210}{x-5}-\frac{210}{x}=1\ \Rightarrow\ 210\cdot5=x(x-5)\ \Rightarrow\ x^2-5x-1050=0\ \Rightarrow\ (x-35)(x+30)=0.$$
So $x=35$.

**Answer: 35**

solutions.title: Guess and check
solutions.body:
$210=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7$. Try planned speed 30 and actual speed 35: times $7$ h and $6$ h, a difference of exactly 1 hour. The equation above has only one positive root, so $x=35$.

**Answer: 35**

prompt: Twenty-five people who always tell the truth or always lie are standing in a queue. The man at the front of the queue says that everyone behind him always lies. Everyone else says that the person immediately in front of them always lies. How many people in the queue always lie?

Four problems were attempted by 100 contestants in a Mathematics competition. The first problem was solved by 90 contestants, the second by 85 contestants, the third by 80 contestants and the fourth by 75 contestants. What is the smallest possible number of contestants who solved all four problems?

solutions.title: Count the failures
solutions.body:
The numbers who failed problems 1 to 4 are $10,15,20,25$, a total of $70$. A contestant who fails several problems is counted several times, so at most $70$ contestants fail something, and at least $100-70=30$ solve all four. This is attainable when the groups of failures are disjoint.

**Answer: 30**

prompt: The 5-digit number '$XX4XY$' is exactly divisible by 165. What is the value of $X+Y$?

solutions.title: Divisibility by 3, 5 and 11
solutions.body:
$165=3\cdot5\cdot11$. Divisible by 5: $Y=0$ or $5$. Divisible by 3: the digit sum $3X+4+Y$ needs $4+Y$ divisible by 3, so $Y=5$. Divisible by 11: alternating digit sum $X-X+4-X+Y=9-X$ must be a multiple of 11, so $X=9$. Check: $99495=165\times603$. Hence $X+Y=14$.

**Answer: 14**

prompt: How many 10-digit numbers are there whose digits are all 1, 2 or 3 and in which adjacent digits differ by 1?

solutions.title: Alternate the middle digit
solutions.body:
A digit 1 or 3 must be followed by 2, while a digit 2 can be followed by 1 or 3. So the digits at odd positions or at even positions are all 2, and the others are free to be 1 or 3. If the first digit is 2, then positions $1,3,5,7,9$ are 2 and positions $2,4,\dots,10$ are free: $2^5=32$ numbers. If the first digit is 1 or 3, positions $2,4,6,8,10$ are all 2 and positions $1,3,5,7,9$ are free but the first must not be 2: $2^5=32$ numbers. Total $32+32=64$.

**Answer: 64**

prompt: In rectangle $JKLM$, the bisector of angle $KJM$ cuts the diagonal $KM$ at point $N$ as shown. The distances between $N$ and sides $LM$ and $KL$ are 8 cm and 1 cm respectively. The length of $KL$ is $(a+\sqrt b)$ cm. What is the value of $a+b$?

solutions.title: Similar triangles
solutions.body:
The bisector of the right angle at $J$ makes $N$ equidistant from $JK$ and $JM$; call this distance $x$. Then $KL=x+8$ (the distance of $N$ from $JK$ plus its distance from $LM$).

Triangle $K$-$N$-(foot on $KL$) has legs $x$ and $1$; triangle $N$-$M$-(foot on $LM$) has legs $8$ and $x$ (the vertical leg is the distance from $N$ to the top side, $x$). They are similar since $N$ lies on $KM$, so $\frac1x=\frac x8$, $x=\sqrt8$. Then $KL=8+\sqrt8$, so $a=8$, $b=8$ and $a+b=16$.

**Answer: 16**

prompt: Numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ are such that $\dfrac{a}{b+c}=\dfrac{b}{c+a}=\dfrac{c}{a+b}=k$. How many possible values of $k$ are there?

solutions.title: Add the three equations
solutions.body:
From $\frac a{b+c}=\frac b{c+a}$ we get $a^2+ac=b^2+bc$, i.e. $(a-b)(a+b+c)=0$. So $a=b$ or $a+b+c=0$; similarly for the other pairs.

If $a+b+c=0$ then $b+c=-a$ and $k=-1$. Otherwise $a=b=c$ and $k=\frac12$. Both occur (e.g. $a=b=c=1$; $a=1,b=2,c=-3$). So there are $2$ values.

**Answer: 2**

prompt: In quadrilateral $ABCD$, $\angle ABC=\angle ADC=90^\circ$, $AD=DC$ and $AB+BC=20$ cm. What is the area in $\text{cm}^2$ of quadrilateral $ABCD$?

solutions.title: Algebra with the diagonal
solutions.body:
Let $AB=x$, $BC=y$, $AC=z$, so $z^2=x^2+y^2=(x+y)^2-2xy=400-4V$ where $V=\frac12xy$ is the area of $ABC$. Triangle $ACD$ is right isosceles with hypotenuse $AC$, so its area is $\frac14z^2=100-V$. The total area is $V+(100-V)=100$.

**Answer: 100**

solutions.title: A special case
solutions.body:
The answer does not depend on the shape, so take the square with $AB=BC=10$: its area is $100$.

**Answer: 100**

prompt: The number $N=3^{16}-1$ has a divisor of 193. It also has some divisors between 75 and 85 inclusive. What is the sum of these divisors?

solutions.title: Factorise
solutions.body:
$N=(3^8-1)(3^8+1)=(3^4-1)(3^4+1)(3^8+1)=80\cdot82\cdot6562$ and $6562=2\cdot17\cdot193$. So $N=2^4\cdot5\cdot2\cdot41\cdot2\cdot17\cdot193=2^6\cdot5\cdot17\cdot41\cdot193$.

Check $75,\dots,85$: $80=2^4\cdot5$, $82=2\cdot41$ and $85=5\cdot17$ divide $N$. The others fail: $75,78,81,84$ need a factor $3$; $77$ needs $7$; $79$, $83$ are primes not dividing $N$; $76$ needs $19$. The sum is $80+82+85=247$.

**Answer: 247**
